title: The Writings
hook: the third part of the Tanakh: poems, wisdom books and stories
carry: they praise, they doubt, they complain

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prophets closed, and the rabbis said the voice passed to the wise, and to fools and children. Your line was the voice goes on. Today the week ends, and the third part of the Bible opens.

Turn the page past Malachi in a Jewish Bible, and the voices change. A king sings to God on a harp. A father teaches his son, and tells the lazy to go and watch the ant. A man covered in sores argues with heaven and won't be comforted. A woman in love searches the city streets at night. A widow gleans barley behind the harvesters. A queen keeps a secret about who she is. Exiles sit by the rivers of Babylon and weep. And almost no one stands up to say thus saith the LORD.

segments.voice: Ketuvim. Writings. The Torah is the teaching, the Prophets are the voice of God through messengers, and the Writings are everything else that was kept. And what's kept is wide. Psalms, the songs and cries that run through the Jewish prayer book. Proverbs, short wisdom about tongues, money and friends. Job, a long argument about suffering that never quite settles. Then short scrolls Jews call megillot, each tied by custom to a season: Song of Songs at Passover, Ruth on Shavuot, Lamentations on Tisha B'Av, Ecclesiastes during Sukkot, Esther on Purim. Then Daniel, Ezra and Nehemiah, and Chronicles. What changes when you cross over? In the Prophets, God mostly speaks to people. In the Writings, people mostly speak: to God, to each other, to themselves. They praise, they doubt, they complain, they fall in love, they grieve a city. Ecclesiastes calls it all vanity. Esther tells its whole story without once naming God. And these books are part of the Bible too: their questions kept right next to the answers. Printed Bibles don't all list them in the same order, and the Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, gives an order of its own. It starts with Ruth, which is where this road goes next. Before it does, look back at a week of endings: Micah's three verbs, a fig tree and no fear, Habakkuk's one line, not by might, hearts turning both ways, and a voice that goes on.

segments.voice: Say the names of the Writings, one for each slow breath, aloud or inside: Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Song of Songs, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, Chronicles. Notice which name catches you, a song, a lament, a love poem, a story, then go back to it and stay there, just the name and the breath. If you pray, one line of a psalm you know can be enough.
Ketuvim. The Writings, the third part of the Bible, where songs, wisdom and stories speak in human voices. Today's word.
Your line: they praise, they doubt, they complain. Here, people mostly do the speaking. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews pray the Psalms daily in the synagogue service and read the short scrolls of the Writings at their festivals, such as Esther on Purim and Ruth on Shavuot.

chat.says: Is every book in the Hebrew Bible God speaking to people?
options: Not all: in the Writings, people mostly speak, to God, to each other, to themselves.
Yes: every book has a prophet saying thus saith the LORD, start to finish.
No: the Writings are later stories that were never counted as Bible.
chat.meaning: In the Prophets God mostly speaks to people; in the Ketuvim, people mostly speak, and these books are part of the Bible too.

Purim.meaning: the festival when the book of Esther is read

notes: Editor pass: Proverbs 6:6 no longer invents 'lazy afternoons'; Ecclesiastes 1:2 now says 'all is vanity' as the text does (not 'much of it is vapor'); dropped the superlative 'plainest'; megillot readings softened to 'tied by custom to a season'; varied the practice opener.

Megillot festival readings (Song of Songs at Passover, Ruth on Shavuot, Lamentations on Tisha B'Av, Ecclesiastes on Sukkot, Esther on Purim) are stated as custom; practice varies (some communities don't read all of them publicly). Keeper please confirm or soften.
'The book of Esther tells its whole story without once naming God' refers to the Hebrew (Masoretic) text; confirm.
Bava Batra 14b order (Ruth, Psalms, Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Lamentations, Daniel, Esther, Ezra, Chronicles) paraphrased only as 'starts with Ruth'; confirm.
'David sings on a harp' is given as 'a king sings to God' without naming David, since Psalm authorship is a tradition claim.
